passage: Dolma, five, woke in the dark flat when the power cut stopped the fan. She hugged her stuffed yak and sang under her breath, the same three-line lullaby, slowly. In the next room her father Anirban heard it and stood at her door without switching on the torch. "Can I sit with you?" he asked. Dolma nodded, still singing, and he hummed the tune quietly until the fan whirred back to life.

qa.q: What did Dolma hold while she sang?
qa.a: A stuffed yak.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she started singing, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Probably fear of the dark after the fan stopped, since she sang under her breath and clung to her toy. She might also have been simply restless, but the timing points to fright.

qa.q: How did Anirban respond in a helpful way?
qa.a: He asked before sitting down and hummed quietly, joining her song only after she nodded. 🤍

qa.q: What might Anirban have been thinking as he stood at the door?
qa.a: Probably that the singing was helping her cope, so he wanted to stay near without taking over. He could also have been unsure whether she wanted company.

grounding: Shows a child singing softly to herself and a toy when frightened, with a parent honouring it and joining when invited.

passage:
"Rehana, why are you whispering to Bunny?" Her mother Jyoti stood in the doorway.
"I'm not whispering. I'm singing."
"Sing louder, then, so I can hear."
"No. It's a quiet song. Bunny is scared of the thunder."
"Is Bunny scared, or are you?"
"Bunny. ...Maybe a little me."
"Can I sing too?"
"You can do the humming part."
Jyoti hummed while the thunder rolled outside, and Rehana's small voice steadied on the last line.

qa.q: Who did Rehana say was scared of the thunder?
qa.a: Bunny.

qa.q: What does Rehana's "Maybe a little me" suggest?
qa.a: She is a bit frightened herself and is using the song for comfort. She may have named Bunny first because that was easier than admitting it.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She asked to join and took only the humming part Rehana offered, so the song stayed Rehana's own comfort.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel hearing "Maybe a little me"?
qa.a: Likely tender and a little concerned, and glad Rehana trusted her with it.

grounding: Shows a child singing quietly to a toy when scared, and a parent joining only when invited.

passage:
Creche note by Sudha, evening carer.
Damini's mother was late today, delayed by traffic. At six, Damini sat in the book corner, holding her teddy, and began to sing very softly: “Chanda mama door ke…” over and over, rocking. She wasn't crying. I didn't interrupt; it seemed to be helping her. After a while she held the teddy out to me and said, “Teddy wants you to sing too.” So I sang with them. When her mother arrived, Damini was humming and calm.

qa.q: Why was Damini's mother late?
qa.a: She was delayed by traffic.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as she sang to her teddy?
qa.a: She was probably lonely and a little worried that her mother was late, and singing helped her feel calm.

qa.q: Why was Sudha right not to interrupt?
qa.a: Singing was Damini's own healthy way of coping, and Sudha joined in only when Damini invited her.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and grateful that Damini found a way to stay calm and that Sudha supported her.

grounding: The carer's note shows a preschooler singing softly to her teddy to soothe herself, and the carer joining when invited.

passage: In the evening, Seema went to milk the buffalo behind the house, and Sahil stayed on the charpai in the courtyard. The lamp flickered. The fields were dark and full of croaking. Sahil pulled his blanket tight and started singing, “Machhli jal ki rani hai,” softly to himself, then a little louder. From the shed came Seema's voice, singing the next line. Sahil sang the line after. They went back and forth until she came out with the warm milk bucket and sat beside him.

qa.q: Where did Seema go in the evening?
qa.a: To milk the buffalo behind the house.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he pulled his blanket tight and began singing?
qa.a: He was probably a bit scared and lonely in the dark courtyard, and singing helped him soothe himself.

qa.q: What did Seema's singing back do for Sahil?
qa.a: It let him know she was near and joined his coping song, so he felt less alone.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had called out “Stop singing, be quiet”?
qa.a: Sahil would lose his way of calming himself and might feel more frightened.

grounding: A child sings to soothe himself when alone and uneasy in the dark, and his mother joins in from nearby.

passage: The drive to Galway took three hours, and the rain didn't stop. In the back seat, Rafael had run out of games. He held his toy dinosaur up to the window and sang to it softly, “Rain, rain, go away, dino wants to play,” making up new verses. Liam, his father, turned the radio off so he could hear. He didn't join in straight away. After the fifth verse Rafael said, “Papa, dino says you sing.” Liam sang the next verse in a deep dino voice.

qa.q: How long did the drive to Galway take?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when he began singing to the dinosaur?
qa.a: He was bored after running out of games, and singing helped him cope with the long, rainy drive.

qa.q: What did Liam do that honoured Rafael's singing?
qa.a: He turned the radio off to listen and waited until Rafael invited him before joining in.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when Rafael invites him to sing?
qa.a: He likely feels touched and happy to be let in, which is why he sings the next verse in a deep dino voice. 😊

grounding: A child sings to his toy to soothe boredom on a long drive, and his father joins in when invited.

passage:
Nap time at the daycare centre. The blinds were down and the other children were asleep. Vijay lay awake, holding his cloth rabbit close, and sang to it very softly, "Chanda mama door ke..."

Anirban, the carer on duty, heard it from the corner. He didn't say "shh." He just sat nearby with his book.

Vijay stopped and looked over. "Do you know the next bit?"

"I do," Anirban whispered. "Shall we sing it quietly together?"

They sang one verse in a whisper. Vijay's eyes began to close.

qa.q: What was Vijay holding close?
qa.a: His cloth rabbit.

qa.q: Why might Vijay be singing to his rabbit at nap time?
qa.a: He was probably feeling lonely or a bit uneasy lying awake while everyone else slept, and singing comforted him. He may also simply have been bored.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Anirban let Vijay keep singing instead of saying "shh", and joined in only when Vijay invited him, which honoured the song as Vijay's way of coping.

qa.q: How does Anirban see Vijay's soft singing?
qa.a: He sees it as a healthy way for Vijay to settle himself, not as noise to stop, so he stays close and waits.

grounding: It shows a child singing softly to a toy to soothe himself at nap time and an adult honouring it and joining in when invited.
